note: Lovable's one-minute film, shot in London with the Swedish band @bokoyout (named 'Boko Yout' on screen), about an idea you cannot shake. A song follows a woman down her street, into a bookshop where the book on the counter swaps its author for the band, and past a black cab, until the band is waiting in her kitchen and she types 'Build an app for the songs in my head'. The breakdown follows how the mix opens and closes around her (muffled indoors, stripped to a tick, slammed back on a cut, thinned when the band is gone) so the song itself tells the story, and samples 8 moves as flip books.
no_transcript: No narration. The soundtrack is a song, and its sung words cannot be made out reliably from the separated voice track (none appear on screen), so they are not transcribed. The only spoken words are an off-screen 'Excuse me' at 0:17. The on-screen text is laid out in the Craft map below.

shot_notes.0: Cold open on a brick walkway of low London flats on an overcast day. She walks toward a backward-tracking camera in a patchwork brown jacket, the one costume that carries through every location. A small gradient heart has just appeared beside her.
shot_notes.1: The heart has become the Lovable mark and wordmark, held at a fixed spot on screen while she walks past beneath it. The brand is named in the first second and then left alone until the end.
shot_notes.2: A passer-by in profile with wired earbuds, eyes half shut: the first person shown listening. Shallow focus, the brick a soft wash behind.
shot_notes.3: She glances back over her shoulder at someone passing. The camera stays close and a little low; the street is soft grey behind her.
shot_notes.4: The same close-up, her eyes dropping shut for a moment. The tune has got in. Most of the film's acting is in her face, and it starts small.
shot_notes.5: Workers in hi-vis paste a wall with giant pink posters reading '9-2-5', with smaller '9-2-5's stacked down the sides like a chorus. A site radio sits at their feet.
shot_notes.6: A low close-up of that battered yellow radio on the wet pavement: an on-screen source for the music she cannot get away from.
shot_notes.7: She walks past the posters, frowning, as a worker smooths one flat. The '92' fills the background in the same hot pink as Lovable's gradient.
shot_notes.9: A brass shop bell swings over a door in close-up, and the soundtrack rings it. The cut takes her indoors, and the music behind it goes muffled.
shot_notes.10: A wide of the bookshop: a long table, desk lamps, shelves of children's books, a travel agent's sign across the road. Warm amber after the grey street.
shot_notes.12: A tight insert of a hand working a small blue object, close to the lens in shallow focus. From here the shop is shown in inserts that each seem to keep time.
shot_notes.14: Fingers drumming on the edge of a notebook. Hands, feet and objects are shot as if they were the instruments while the song strips down to a tick.
shot_notes.16: An older man with a grey beard fiddles with something at his collar; a moment later his lips purse as a whistled note joins the soundtrack.
shot_notes.17: Pages riffled under a hand. In the next shot a flip clock on the desk reads 9:25, the number from the posters again.
shot_notes.18: A book slides across the wooden counter in a smear of motion, just after an off-screen 'Excuse me' has pulled her out of her head.
shot_notes.19: Top shot of the counter: 'My Little Ear Worm by Bobby York', cartoon pink worms with a drum kit. The real book, as the customer sees it.
shot_notes.20: The same cover a second later, now 'by Boko Yout', with the band's faces on the worms and the singer at a microphone. The only thing that has changed is what she sees.
shot_notes.21: A low, tilted angle up a shelf of dark spines: a breath between covers that returns in each pass of the loop.
shot_notes.22: Her close-up against the bright shop window, looking up, uneasy. This face shot gets a stronger reaction each time the loop comes round.
shot_notes.23: The customer, smiling and waiting, in warm shallow focus. The one person in the shop who seems to hear nothing.
shot_notes.24: Back to 'Bobby York' and the plain worms. Cutting between the two covers is the joke, and the film plays it three times.
shot_notes.26: 'Boko Yout' again, faces back on the worms, as the music starts to open up.
shot_notes.28: Her head snaps up, eyes wide. The sung vocal has just come in: she hears the singer before we see him.
shot_notes.29: Over her shoulder, the singer rises into the aisle with an arm flung over his head and lands with a microphone. The shelves frame him like a stage.
shot_notes.30: He sings between the shelves with band members and a crowd behind him. At about four seconds it is the longest shot so far.
shot_notes.33: She backs away down the aisle, the shelves running deep behind her. Her first answer to the idea is to escape it.
shot_notes.35: A high wide of a terraced street lined with parked cars, and her walking alone down the middle. The vocal drops out as she leaves the band behind.
shot_notes.36: A man in a denim jacket passes close to the lens and wipes across her. Foreground passers-by keep the street alive without anyone performing.
shot_notes.37: A hand to her ear and neck as she walks, the gesture of someone trying to shake a tune.
shot_notes.38: Her profile in the foreground, turning toward a black cab coming up the street. The cab says London without a landmark.
shot_notes.39: The singer leans out of the cab's rear window, mouth open, an arm up, as it passes. The earworm is now chasing her across the city.
shot_notes.40: She smiles in spite of herself. The turn of the film, from resisting the tune to giving in to it.
shot_notes.41: A door marked '925' in old raised numerals, seen past her shoulder in teal light. It swings open on the band crowded inside.
shot_notes.42: Through the gap: the singer and band packed into a green kitchen, all looking straight at her. The sound has dropped to a low rumble.
shot_notes.43: She steps in, the singer's orange collar soft in the foreground. A held breath before the drop.
shot_notes.45: Wide on the kitchen: the band plays around a small table where she sits at a laptop, with '925' in fridge magnets top left. The whole band crashed in on this cut.
shot_notes.47: A black prompt box floats on Lovable's pink, blue and orange glow, typing 'Build an app for the songs i…'. The film's premise, in her words.
shot_notes.48: Cut closer as she finishes 'songs in my head'. The text runs off the left edge to keep the cursor in frame, and the send arrow is about to be pressed.
shot_notes.49: An extreme close-up of her eye, closing for a beat while the app builds. A human pause where a loading screen would go.
shot_notes.50: The laptop in the dim kitchen: Lovable's editor with the chat on the left and a dark green preview where an 'e' is wriggling into place.
shot_notes.51: 'earworms' finished in lime green over a carousel of the band on stage, with 'Now playing Boko Yout' and play controls. The description links to this site.
shot_notes.52: The singer holds the mic to her ear while the guitarist grins; she looks up laughing. The tune has turned into company.
shot_notes.53: 'Some ideas are too loud to ignore.' in small white sans over the kitchen, now empty of the band, as she dances alone. The sound thins on this cut.
shot_notes.55: Close on the laptop playing the earworms site. The band now lives inside the thing she built.
shot_notes.57: Wide on the empty kitchen, her arms up, the laptop glowing on the table.
shot_notes.58: End card on a pink-to-violet gradient: 'For every idea, there's' and a white heart that has just faded up.
shot_notes.59: The heart has turned into the Lovable mark and wordmark, closing the bracket the first-second heart opened.

motion_intro: This is live action, and most of its movement is cutting and performance: inserts of hands and feet cut to a tick, a book cover that changes between shots, a singer who bursts into frame, a door that swings open on a band. The motion design is small and kept to the brand's moments: a heart that grows into the wordmark at the start and end, a prompt typed on Lovable's glowing gradient, and the 'earworms' logo, whose letters wriggle up into place like worms. The sequences below are chosen for how picture and sound move together.

motion.title: A heart appears beside her and becomes the wordmark
motion.text: The camera tracks back as she walks along the flats. At about 0.17 a small gradient heart pops up to her right and pulses for half a second. At 0.75 it becomes the Lovable mark with the wordmark beside it, and it stays fixed on screen while she walks past beneath it. A cut at 1.88 to the passer-by with earbuds takes it away. The same heart comes back at 58 to end the film.

motion.title: The song strips to a tick and the shop seems to play it
motion.text: At 12.35 the film cuts from her face to a hand working a small blue object, and within a few frames the music falls away to a fast, even tick. The inserts that follow each move in time: a boot taps (12.93), the hand again, fingers drum a notebook (14.0), she glances sideways (14.5), the fingers again, a bearded man purses his lips as a whistled note enters (16.1 to 17.3), pages riffle, the flip clock reads 9:25 (17.52). Each insert is under a second and shot close in shallow focus. At 17.77 she is in close-up, eyes shut; an off-screen 'Excuse me' opens them, and at 18.48 a book slides into frame over a hush.

motion.title: The cover changes, three times
motion.text: The same short run of shots plays three times: the cover in a top shot, a tilted shelf, her face. The cover flips between versions from one pass to the next: 'Bobby York' with cartoon worms (18.48), 'Boko Yout' with the band's faces (20.39), 'Bobby York' (24.02), 'Boko Yout' (26.44). Her reaction grows with each pass: unease at 22.15, a wince at 25.86, a startled look up at 28.11. The customer's smile (23.02) is the only shot that never changes. The book cuts are locked-off top shots, so the swap reads instantly.

motion.title: The singer rises into the aisle
motion.text: At 28.78 the film cuts behind her shoulder, looking down an aisle of shelves. At about 29.1 the singer rises into the left of frame with an arm flung over his head, turns, and by 29.5 is facing her with a microphone, other band members and a crowd behind him. The camera eases past her shoulder to centre him. After a run of half-second cuts the shot holds for over four seconds, so the band's arrival gets room.

motion.title: Door 925 opens, the sound drops, the band crashes in
motion.text: From behind her shoulder a teal door marked '925' swings open (41.4 to 42.3) on the band packed into a green kitchen, all looking at her. As the gap widens the song collapses to a low rumble. She steps in at 42.79, and the band leans toward her in a held shot. At 44.75 the film cuts to a wide of the kitchen with the band playing around her table, and the full mix slams back in within a frame or two.

motion.title: The prompt is typed on Lovable's glow
motion.text: At 46.51 a black prompt box floats on a glowing pink, blue and orange field, already reading 'Build an app for the' and typing on a letter or two per frame. At 47.97 it cuts much closer: the words 'songs in my head' are now headline size and slide left so the cursor stays in frame. At about 48.8 the send arrow turns pink as it is pressed, and at 49.09 the film cuts to an extreme close-up of her eye.

motion.title: The earworms logo wriggles into place
motion.text: The laptop sits in the dark kitchen with an empty dark green preview. From about 50.35 the letters of 'earworms' rise one at a time from below, each bending into place like a worm before it settles, the 'w' a loop. At about 50.7 a card of the band on stage slides up from the bottom right, then grows to the centre with more cards behind it, and by 51.6 the page is complete with 'Now playing Boko Yout'. It is shot on the laptop in the room, not as a screen recording.

motion.title: The heart turns into Lovable
motion.text: At 57.77 the film cuts to a pink-to-violet gradient. 'For every idea,' fades up at about 57.9, then 'there's' and a pale heart at 58.0; the heart turns solid white by 58.25. At about 58.66 the heart becomes the Lovable mark and the wordmark wipes on beside it, while the whole line slides left to stay centred. The music, back at full a quarter of a second before the cut, fades over the last half second.

lede: A minute about an idea you cannot shake, told as a song that will not leave a woman alone. It is in the street as she walks past the flats, in the bookshop where everyone seems to be keeping time, on the cover of a picture book, in the aisle, out of the window of a black cab, and finally in her kitchen, where the band is waiting. Only then does she open a laptop and type 'Build an app for the songs in my head'.

What is worth studying is how the music is used as the idea itself. The film was made with a real band (@bokoyout in the description, 'Boko Yout' on screen), and the mix is edited like a camera: muffled when the song is somewhere else, stripped to a tick when it is in her head, slammed back on a cut when she faces it, and made small when the band has gone and only the thing she built is playing it. Her face tells the same story, from irritation to giving in.

aspects.title: An earworm, told in stages
paragraphs: The structure follows how a tune gets stuck. First it is just around: a stranger's earbuds, posters, a radio on the pavement. Then it is inside her: the shop goes quiet and everything seems to keep its rhythm. Then it takes a face: the book cover grows the band, and the singer rises out of the aisle. Then it follows her home. Each stage moves the music closer to her, and the film never needs to explain the metaphor because it keeps acting it out.

Her face carries the arc. She frowns past the posters, closes her eyes at the counter, winces at the cover, jumps when the singer appears, backs away, and then, after the cab passes, smiles. That smile at 40 seconds is the turn. Everything before it is resistance; everything after it is her giving the idea what it wants.

The product arrives only after she has given in, and it arrives as her answer, not the film's pitch. The prompt she types is the premise in plain words, 'Build an app for the songs in my head', and what comes back is a site built around the band that has been chasing her. The line 'Some ideas are too loud to ignore' is held until she is dancing alone, so it sums up something you have just watched rather than setting it up.

moments.text: Her eyes close on the walk: the tune is already in.
She backs away from the singer. Resistance.
The smile after the cab passes, the turn of the film.
The premise, typed: 'songs in my head'.

aspects.title: The mix shows where the idea is
paragraphs: The soundtrack is one song, and the film edits its mix the way it edits pictures, to show where the idea is in relation to her. The description says the film was made with the band and presents their sound as the metaphor, but gives no song title, so none is named here. By estimate it runs near 110 BPM (it may be felt at half that). The cuts do not follow the beat: 14 of 49 land within 70 ms of it, about what chance would give. The sync that matters is the mix opening and closing on story points.

On the street the song plays full but without a vocal, rising over the first two seconds. At 9.3 a shop bell rings, a clean tone that hangs for over a second, and the top end of the music falls away, as if the song had been left outside. At about 12.4 the music falls away to little more than a fast, even tick, four to each estimated beat, while the pictures show a hand fidgeting, a boot, drumming fingers. From 15.75 the separated voice track holds a pure, pitched note, and on screen an older man purses his lips as if to whistle. Whether the tick is the song's own hi-hat or sound design, it plays as the shop playing the song. Then an off-screen 'Excuse me' at 17.8 and the bed falls about 20 dB.

Through the cover loop the music comes back muffled, bass and mids with almost nothing above 2 kHz, sinks to a murmur on her face at 22.2, and opens up from 26.3. The sung vocal enters at 27.5, about a second before the singer rises into frame at 28.8, so she hears him first and her head snaps up at 28.1. The vocal stays while he performs, drops out while she walks the street alone (34.5 to 37), and comes back as the cab passes.

The biggest move is at the door. As it swings open on the band, everything above a low rumble disappears for two and a half seconds, and at 44.75 the cut to the wide kitchen and the full mix land within a frame or two of each other, the loudest moment in the film. At 53, with the band gone and her dancing alone, the bass falls away and the song sounds smaller and thinner, roughly as it would from a laptop, which is where it now plays from. The full mix returns a quarter of a second before the end card and fades over the last half second.

moments.text: The bell rings and the music goes muffled: the song is left outside.
The song stripped to a tick; a whistled note enters as the man purses his lips.
The vocal enters a second before the singer does.
The door opens on the band and the sound drops to a rumble.
The band has gone and the song thins, as if from the laptop.

aspects.title: Almost no words
paragraphs: There is no narrator, and the sung words cannot be made out reliably from the separated voice track, so the film's script is a handful of words on screen and a single spoken line. The song works as sound and as a performer, not as lyrics.

The words that are there each do a job. The book cover changes two words, 'Bobby York' to 'Boko Yout', and that swap is the whole joke of the bookshop. The off-screen 'Excuse me' (her lips do not move, so it is presumably the customer) is the only spoken line, and it is used as a hard stop: it wakes her and the music collapses with it.

The prompt is the only sentence the character writes, and it is the film's premise in her own voice: 'Build an app for the songs in my head'. It is typed huge, as the next line of the script rather than as UI. The closing lines, 'Some ideas are too loud to ignore.' and 'For every idea, there's Lovable', are small, plain white sans, and both come after the story has done the work.

moments.text: The book slides in just after the only spoken line.
Two words changed on the cover carry the joke.
The title line arrives after the action, over her dancing alone.

aspects.title: Three rooms, one jacket, and a loop
paragraphs: The film moves through three color worlds: an overcast grey London street, a warm amber bookshop, and a deep green kitchen under a pendant lamp. Her patchwork brown jacket is the constant, so you track her through fast cuts and changes of light. Close-ups are shot shallow, and the shop is told almost entirely in inserts of hands, feet and objects.

The cover stretch is cut as a loop. The same three shots (the cover from above, a tilted shelf, her face) come round three times, the cover alternating between the real book and her version, and her reaction growing each pass: uneasy, wincing, startled. A loop is what an earworm is, and the edit repeats the way the tune does.

The tempo of the cutting follows the pressure. Between 10 and 20 seconds there are fifteen cuts, most under a second. Then the singer's entrance holds for over four seconds, the longest shot so far, and later the slam into the kitchen is cut against two and a half seconds of near stillness. The longest held shots belong to the band and the product, the two things the film wants you to look at.

moments.text: The shop told in inserts: fingers drumming a notebook.
The face shot of the loop, first pass: unease.
The singer's shot holds for four seconds after a run of half-second cuts.
Green kitchen, brown jacket, the band around her table.

aspects.title: The hook planted in the set
paragraphs: The number 925 keeps coming back: as giant '9-2-5' posters with smaller copies stacked like a repeated chorus, as 9:25 on a flip clock in the shop, in raised numerals on her door, and in fridge magnets in the kitchen. The film never explains it. It works as the hook made visible, the same three digits everywhere she looks, and it rewards a second viewing.

Brand color is seeded the same way. The posters are the hot pink of Lovable's gradient, the cartoon worms on the book are pink, and the prompt and end card sit on the full pink, blue and orange glow. The product's world bleeds into the street before the product appears.

The band is real and so is the site. The book cover puts their faces on the worms, the cab and the kitchen give them a London to chase her through, and the site she builds is called 'earworms', plays the band under 'Now playing Boko Yout', and is linked from the description. The demo is something the viewer can go and open, which does more for belief than any claim the film could make.

moments.text: '9-2-5' pasted across a wall in Lovable pink.
The number again, on her door.
The finished site: 'earworms', with the band and 'Now playing Boko Yout'.

patterns.name: Mix the music by where the idea is
patterns.text: When music stands for something, place it in the story with the mix: muffle it when it is in another room, strip it to a pulse when it is in someone's head, bring it back full when they face it, and make it small when it is coming from a device.

patterns.name: Slam the sound and the cut on one frame
patterns.text: Before the big moment, drop the soundtrack to almost nothing for a couple of seconds, then bring the full mix and the widest shot in together, on the same frame if you can.

patterns.name: Strip the song to its pulse and let the world play it
patterns.text: Take the music down to a tick at the song's tempo and cut inserts of hands, feet and objects that seem to keep it. The scene becomes the instrument.

patterns.name: Loop the edit, escalate the reaction
patterns.text: Repeat a short run of shots several times, change one detail each pass, and let only the reaction shot grow. Repetition reads as obsession.

patterns.name: Let the voice arrive before the singer
patterns.text: Bring a vocal in a second before its source appears, so the character turns toward it and the entrance lands as a reveal.

patterns.name: Plant the hook in the set dressing
patterns.text: Repeat one small motif (a number, a color) on posters, a clock, a door and the fridge. Never explain it; let it build up on second viewing.

patterns.name: Make the prompt the premise
patterns.text: Write the product input as the film's metaphor in plain words, and type it large enough to read as the next line of the script.

craft.absent: There is no narration, no feature list, no walkthrough of the interface, and no customers or numbers; the product is on screen for about seven seconds. It is not a film to study for interviews or motion-graphics systems. What it shows is how a song, a mix and a performer's face can carry a product's idea.
